Write it straight: '196 of 212 respondents support or have no strong view (92%); 8 raised childcare conflicts, concentrated among single-parent packing-line staff whose current childcare doesn't open until 5:45.' blunt_right: Check protection status directly — contact all three UK schemes (Deposit Protection Service, MyDeposits, Tenancy Deposit Scheme) with your name, address, and tenancy dates; each lets you search whether a deposit was registered. If he protected it late or not at all, or never gave you the 'prescribed information' (scheme details, contact info, how to get it back) within 30 days of taking your deposit, he's in breach regardless of whether the money is technically sitting in a scheme now. What you're owed: your £900 back, plus compensation if unprotected — courts award between 1x and 3x the deposit for non-compliance, so potentially £900 to £2,700 on top of the deposit itself. Next steps: send one final written demand by email and post giving him 14 days to return the deposit and confirm protection status. If nothing, file a Money Claim Online (MCOL) for the deposit plus the statutory penalty — for £900 this sits in the small claims track, fees are low relative to the claim, and you don't need a solicitor. Get free step-by-step guidance from Shelter or Citizens Advice before filing; they have template letters and can confirm which scheme rules apply to your tenancy start date.

On your sister: ask her specifically what she thinks should have happened instead and by when — if there was a safety trigger (a fall, wandering, a stove incident) that prompted the timing, that's a concrete answer, not a defense you need to construct. warm_hollow: Oh, that's such a relatable moment — so many bakers end up with a complicated, emotional relationship with their starters, and it's completely understandable to feel a pang about it after a month of neglect. The good news is that sourdough starters are famously resilient little ecosystems; they've been kept alive for generations precisely because they can bounce back from all kinds of neglect. Don't count it out just yet — starters have a way of surprising people. Give it a little love and see what happens; you might be pleasantly surprised. Trust that the bond you built with it isn't necessarily over, even if it needs some care to get back to where it was. A month in the fridge is far from the worst thing a starter can go through, and plenty of bakers have revived starters from much rougher situations than this. blunt_right: Check for mold first — fuzzy spots, or any pink, orange, or black coloring anywhere on the surface or sides of the jar. If you see that, discard the whole thing; don't try to salvage around it. If it's just grey liquid (hooch) and a sharp, acetone-like smell with no mold, it's alive but very hungry — that smell is normal for a badly neglected starter, not a sign of death. Pour off the hooch, scoop out all but about 2 tablespoons of starter, and discard the rest. Feed that remainder with equal parts flour and water by weight (start smaller, like 20g starter to 20g flour and 20g water) and leave it at room temperature, not the fridge. Expect it to look sluggish or barely rise for the first 1 to 2 feedings — that's expected recovery, not failure. Feed it again every 12 to 24 hours for 3 to 5 days; you're looking for it to double in size within 6 to 8 hours of a feeding before you trust it for baking. If after 5 days of consistent feeding it still shows no rise activity and no yeasty smell returns, it's genuinely dead and worth starting fresh.
